title: Ἀνὴρ ναυαγός
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 53 (= Perry 30). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀνὴρ πλούσιος Ἀθηναῖος μεθ’ ἑτέρων τινῶν ἔπλει.
sentences.tr: Anēr plousios Athēnaios meth' heterōn tinōn eplei.
sentences.l: A rich Athenian man was sailing with certain others.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ χειμῶνος σφοδροῦ γενομένου καὶ τῆς νηὸς περιτραπείσης, οἱ μὲν λοιποὶ πάντες διενήχοντο, ὁ δὲ Ἀθηναῖος παρ’ ἕκαστα τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν ἐπικαλούμενος μυρία ἐπηγγέλλετο, εἰ περισωθείη.
sentences.tr: Kai dē cheimōnos sphodrou genomenou kai tēs nēos peritrapeisēs, hoi men loipoi pantes dienēchonto, ho de Athēnaios par' hekasta tēn Athēnan epikaloumenos myria epēngelleto, ei perisōtheiē.
sentences.l: And when a violent storm had arisen and the ship had been overturned, all the rest were swimming across, but the Athenian, calling on Athena at every moment, kept promising countless things, if he should be brought safely through.
sentences.i: A violent storm came on and the ship capsized; all the rest struck out swimming, but the Athenian, calling on Athena at every turn, kept promising her countless offerings if only he came through alive.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes set the scene (χειμῶνος γενομένου, τῆς νηὸς περιτραπείσης) before the μέν … δέ divides the swimmers from the shouter. διανήχομαι is to swim across or through. εἰ περισωθείη is an optative: the condition as he framed it to himself. Athena is the patron goddess of Athens, so an Athenian calls on her by right; μυρία is 'countless things' — the offerings are left unnamed and unnumbered.

sentences.t: Εἷς δέ τις τῶν συννεναυαγηκότων παρανηχόμενος ἔφη πρὸς αὐτόν· « Σὺν Ἀθηνᾷ καὶ σὺ χεῖρα κινεῖ. »
sentences.tr: Heis de tis tōn synnenauagēkotōn paranēchomenos ephē pros auton· « Syn Athēnāi kai sy cheira kinei. »
sentences.l: And one of those shipwrecked along with him, swimming beside him, said to him: « Along with Athena, move your own hand too. »
sentences.i: One of his fellow castaways, swimming alongside, said to him: « With Athena's help — and move your own hand too. »
sentences.n: σὺν Ἀθηνᾷ καὶ χεῖρα κίνει was a current Greek proverb, and the fable is built around it. καὶ σύ, 'you too', sets the man's hand beside the goddess's help rather than in place of it. συννεναυαγηκότων is a perfect participle: those who have been through the wreck with him.

sentences.t: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς μετὰ τῆς τῶν θεῶν παρακλήσεως χρὴ καὶ αὐτούς τι ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν λογιζομένους δρᾶν.
sentences.tr: Atar oun kai hēmas meta tēs tōn theōn paraklēseōs chrē kai autous ti hyper autōn logizomenous dran.
sentences.l: And so we too, along with our calling on the gods, must ourselves think out something on our own behalf and do it.
sentences.i: And so we too, while calling on the gods, must think of something to do for ourselves as well.
sentences.n: Chambry prints three closing morals here, one after another; all three belong to the text as it has come down and none is trimmed. Ἀτὰρ οὖν καί, 'and so, for our part', is not one of the standard closing formulas. λογιζομένους carries the reckoning and δρᾶν the doing: think, then act.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ἀγαπητόν ἐστι καὶ ἐνεργοῦντας θεῶν εὐνοίας τυγχάνειν ἢ ἑαυτῶν ἀμελοῦντας ὑπὸ τῶν δαιμόνων περισῴζεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Hoti agapēton esti kai energountas theōn eunoias tynchanein ē heautōn amelountas hypo tōn daimonōn perisōizesthai.
sentences.l: That it is a more welcome thing to obtain the gods' goodwill while also working oneself, than, neglecting oneself, to be brought safely through by the divine powers.
sentences.i: That it is better to win the gods' goodwill while working oneself than to be rescued by the divine powers while neglecting oneself.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the 'the story shows' is unexpressed in the Greek, which opens simply 'That…'. ἀγαπητόν … ἤ carries a comparison though no comparative word stands in the Greek; 'more to be welcomed than' is the sense, and the degree is a judgement, not a certainty. τυγχάνω takes the genitive of what one obtains (εὐνοίας). δαίμονες here are simply the gods, without the darker colouring the word took on later.

sentences.t: Τοὺς εἰς συμφορὰς ἐμπίπτοντας χρὴ καὶ αὐτοὺς ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῶν κοπιᾶν καὶ οὕτω τοῦ θεοῦ περὶ βοηθείας δέεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Tous eis symphoras empiptontas chrē kai autous hyper heautōn kopian kai houtō tou theou peri boētheias deesthai.
sentences.l: Those who fall into misfortunes must themselves also toil on their own behalf, and so ask the god for help.
sentences.n: χρή with the accusative and infinitive: 'it is necessary that those falling… toil'. δέομαι takes the genitive of the person asked (τοῦ θεοῦ), with περί for the matter asked about.
